definition: to try to equal or be like someone you admire

examples.text: Young republics often tried to emulate the constitution of an older, stable neighbor.
Engineers emulate the shape of a kingfisher's beak to design quieter trains.
My little brother emulates everything I do, right down to how I tie my shoes.

confused.note: To imitate is simply to copy; to emulate is to copy out of admiration, hoping to match or surpass.

questions.passage: As a teenager, the violinist kept a poster of Itzhak Perlman above her music stand. She studied his recordings for hours, hoping to ______ the warmth of his tone and the ease of his bowing.
questions.explanation: She admired him and worked to match his playing.

distractors.why: Disparage means to belittle, but she admired his playing.
Repudiate means to reject firmly, the opposite of trying to match something.
Elucidate means to explain; she wanted to reproduce his tone, not explain it.

definition: suggesting that something bad is going to happen

examples.text: The story opens with an ominous silence in a house that is usually full of noise.
An ominous crack appeared in the ice shelf weeks before it collapsed.
Ominous gray clouds gathered just as we spread out the picnic blanket.

confused.note: Ominous means threatening; omnipresent means present everywhere.

questions.passage: The hikers had planned to reach the ridge by noon. But the sudden drop in temperature and the ______ rumble of thunder from the west convinced them to turn back at once.
questions.explanation: Thunder that convinces hikers to retreat is a threatening sign.

distractors.why: Auspicious means promising good fortune, which would not send them back.
Mundane means ordinary and dull; this thunder was alarming.
Ephemeral means short-lived, which does not explain why they turned back.

definition: kept secret or done secretly, often because it is not allowed

examples.text: Clandestine printing presses kept the resistance newspaper in circulation.
The lovers arrange a clandestine meeting in the orchard after midnight.
We held a clandestine planning session for Mom's surprise party in the garage.

confused.note: Clandestine stresses planned secrecy; surreptitious stresses quick, sneaky action.

questions.passage: Officially the two rival firms had no contact. Unofficially, their chief engineers held ______ meetings in a rented warehouse, sharing designs that neither company's board knew existed.
questions.explanation: Meetings hidden from both boards are planned and secret.

distractors.why: Overt means open and public, but nobody knew of these meetings.
Perfunctory means done as a dull routine; the passage stresses secrecy.
Futile means pointless, but the engineers did share designs.

definition: very attentive to detail and hard to please

examples.text: The lab's fastidious technician rejects any slide with a single speck of dust.
The detective is a fastidious man who straightens every picture frame he passes.
My aunt is fastidious about her kitchen and alphabetizes the spice rack.

confused.note: Meticulous is praise for careful work; fastidious can suggest being fussy and hard to satisfy.

questions.passage: The translator was famously ______. She was known to spend an entire afternoon on a single sentence and once delayed a book's publication for a month because she was unhappy with one comma.
questions.explanation: Delaying a book over a comma shows extreme, hard-to-satisfy attention to detail.

distractors.why: Cursory means hasty and shallow, the opposite of an afternoon on one sentence.
Prolific means producing a great deal; someone this slow is not turning out much.
Impetuous means acting quickly without thought, the reverse of her slow care.

definition: to calm a fear or worry, or make it less strong

examples.text: The governor toured the harbor to allay fears that the port would close.
The study's large sample size should allay doubts about its conclusions.
The vet's calm voice allayed my worries about the puppy's limp.

confused.note: Allay means to calm a fear; an ally is a friend or partner.

questions.passage: Parents had been alarmed by rumors that the school's drinking water was unsafe. To ______ their concerns, the principal released the full laboratory results, which showed the water met every standard.
questions.explanation: Releasing reassuring test results is meant to calm the parents' worry.

distractors.why: Exacerbate means to make worse, the opposite of the principal's goal.
Corroborate means to confirm; the results showed the concerns were unfounded.
Elicit means to draw out; the principal wanted to settle the concerns, not produce them.

definition: to accept or agree to something without arguing, often unwillingly

examples.text: Facing a larger army, the duke acquiesced to the terms of the treaty.
Tired of quarreling, the heroine acquiesces to her aunt's plan for the summer.
I wanted pizza, but I acquiesced when everyone else voted for tacos.

confused.note: Acquiesce means to give in quietly; acquaint means to make familiar.

questions.passage: The lead actor disliked the new ending and said so at the first rehearsal. When it became clear that the director would not change her mind, however, he ______ and learned the revised lines.
questions.explanation: He stopped objecting and went along with the decision.

distractors.why: Dissented means disagreed openly, which he had done earlier but then stopped doing.
Gloated means took smug pleasure in one's own success, which makes no sense for someone who lost the argument.
Digressed means wandered off the topic, which does not describe giving in.

definition: not well known, or hard to understand

examples.text: She built her career on an obscure poet whose work had been out of print for a century.
The origins of the festival are obscure, since no early records survive.
The instructions were so obscure that we gave up and watched a video.

confused.note: Obscure can mean little known or unclear; abstruse means hard to understand because it is complex.

questions.passage: Before the documentary aired, the composer was ______: her scores sat unplayed in a university basement, and even specialists in the period had rarely heard her name.
questions.explanation: Unplayed scores and an unfamiliar name show she was little known.

distractors.why: Eminent means famous and respected, the opposite of her status then.
Prolific means producing much work; the sentence is about fame, not output.
Notorious means famous for something bad, but she was simply unknown.

definition: ordinary and not interesting

examples.text: The novel finds beauty in mundane tasks like folding laundry and waiting for a bus.
Most of a field biologist's day is mundane work such as labeling sample bags.
After a week at the beach, homework and chores felt painfully mundane.

confused.note: Mundane means everyday and routine; banal means so unoriginal that it is boring.

questions.passage: Viewers who expect a spy's life to be full of car chases may be disappointed by the memoir. Most of its chapters describe ______ work: filling out expense forms, waiting in parked cars, and reading reports.
questions.explanation: Forms, waiting, and reports are ordinary, unexciting tasks.

distractors.why: Clandestine means secret; the contrast is with excitement, and forms are simply dull.
Ominous means threatening, which does not describe paperwork.
Arduous means requiring great effort, but these tasks are dull, not strenuous.

definition: to cause a feeling, situation, or condition to exist

examples.text: Decades of unfair taxes engendered deep resentment among the farmers.
Sharing data openly engenders trust between research teams.
The coach's honesty engendered loyalty in her players.

confused.note: Engender means to give rise to; endanger means to put at risk.

questions.passage: The new manager's habit of taking credit for her team's ideas did not go unnoticed. Within months it had ______ so much resentment that three senior designers asked to be transferred.
questions.explanation: Her habit caused resentment to arise.

distractors.why: Allayed means calmed, but the resentment grew.
Precluded means prevented, yet the resentment clearly developed.
Emulated means imitated, which does not fit causing a feeling.

definition: producing a large amount of work, fruit, or offspring

examples.text: A prolific novelist, she published forty books in thirty years.
Rabbits are prolific breeders, which is why the island population exploded.
Our tomato plants were so prolific that we gave bags of tomatoes to the neighbors.

confused.note: Prolific means highly productive; profligate means wildly wasteful.

questions.passage: Schubert died at thirty-one, yet he was astonishingly ______: he left behind more than six hundred songs, nine symphonies, and a large body of chamber music.
questions.explanation: Hundreds of works in a short life show he produced a great deal.

distractors.why: Fastidious means fussy about details; the evidence given is about quantity.
Obscure means little known, which the list of works does not address.
Reticent means reluctant to speak, which is unrelated to how much he composed.

definition: wise and showing good judgment

examples.text: The sagacious queen kept her kingdom out of a war that ruined her neighbors.
In the fable, a sagacious old turtle settles every quarrel in the pond.
My grandfather gave me the sagacious advice to sleep on any big decision.

confused.note: A sage is a wise person; sagacious is the adjective for the same quality.

questions.passage: Investors praised the firm's founder as ______. While competitors rushed to expand during the boom, she quietly set aside cash, and when the market fell her company was one of the few able to keep its staff.
questions.explanation: Saving during a boom and surviving the fall shows wisdom and good judgment.

distractors.why: Impetuous means acting rashly, which describes the competitors, not her.
Ostentatious means showy, but she acted quietly.
Gullible means easily fooled, the opposite of her foresight.

definition: never having happened or existed before

examples.text: The 1918 flu spread at an unprecedented speed along wartime shipping routes.
The new telescope captured distant galaxies in unprecedented detail.
Our team's ten wins in a row are unprecedented in the school's history.

confused.note: Unprecedented means it has never happened before; unparalleled means nothing equals it.

questions.passage: The museum had never before lent a single item from its founder's collection. Its decision to send forty paintings abroad for a year was therefore ______, and it surprised even longtime members of the staff.
questions.explanation: The museum had never done this before.

distractors.why: Habitual means done regularly as a habit, but this had never happened.
Surreptitious means sneaky and secret; the loan was a public decision.
Inadvertent means accidental, but the loan was a deliberate decision.

definition: more than is needed; unnecessary

examples.text: The editor cut every superfluous adjective from the opening chapter.
The second backup pump proved superfluous, since the first never failed.
With the map on my phone, the paper atlas in the glove box seemed superfluous.

confused.note: Superfluous means more than needed; superficial means shallow or only on the surface.

questions.passage: The architect believed that a building should contain nothing ______. She removed decorative columns that held up no weight and eliminated a second staircase that led to the same floor as the first.
questions.explanation: Columns that support nothing and a duplicate staircase are unnecessary extras.

distractors.why: Indispensable means absolutely necessary, the opposite of what she removed.
Austere means severely plain; she favored plainness and removed excess, not plainness itself.
Ambiguous means unclear in meaning, which does not describe extra columns.

definition: known or understood by only a few people

examples.text: Only a handful of clerks understood the arcane rules of the royal treasury.
The wizard's library is full of arcane texts in forgotten alphabets.
My uncle loves the arcane details of baseball statistics from the 1920s.

confused.note: Arcane means known to few; archaic means very old or old-fashioned.

questions.passage: The rules governing how the legislature schedules a vote are so ______ that even veteran lawmakers must consult the chamber's parliamentarian, one of the few people who has mastered them.
questions.explanation: Rules that only a few specialists have mastered are known to few.

distractors.why: Lucid means clear and easy to understand, the opposite of these rules.
Mundane means ordinary; the passage stresses how few people understand the rules.
Arbitrary means without reason; the rules may be hard to learn but are not described as random.

definition: done quickly and without attention to detail

examples.text: A cursory look at the data missed the error that a careful review later caught.
The inspector gave the ship only a cursory check before it sailed.
I gave the contract a cursory read and almost missed the cancellation fee.

confused.note: Cursory means quick and shallow; cursive is joined handwriting.

questions.passage: The safety board concluded that the inspection had been ______ at best. The inspector had spent four minutes in a factory with two hundred machines and had not opened a single electrical panel.
questions.explanation: Four minutes for two hundred machines is a hasty, shallow inspection.

distractors.why: Exhaustive means complete and thorough, the opposite of this inspection.
Clandestine means secret, which the passage does not suggest.
Scrupulous means extremely careful, which this inspector was not.

definition: not done on purpose; accidental

examples.text: An inadvertent change in temperature spoiled the first batch of samples.
The clerk's inadvertent omission of one name left a family off the land records.
My inadvertent "reply all" sent the joke to the entire school staff.

confused.note: Inadvertent describes an action done by accident; inattentive describes a person who is not paying attention.

questions.passage: The museum insists that the damage was ______. According to its report, a technician brushed the canvas with her sleeve while adjusting a light and did not realize what had happened until later.
questions.explanation: She touched the canvas by accident and did not even know.

distractors.why: Deliberate means done on purpose, which the report denies.
Negligible means too small to matter; the report is about intent, not size.
Ominous means threatening, which does not describe an accident.

definition: harmful or damaging

examples.text: Too much salt in the soil has a deleterious effect on most crops.
The long blockade had deleterious consequences for the city's trade.
Staying up past midnight had a deleterious effect on my morning quiz scores.

confused.note: Deleterious means harmful; delirious means wildly excited or confused.

questions.passage: Early studies suggested that the pesticide was safe for bees. Later research showed that even small doses had ______ effects, weakening the insects' memory and making it harder for them to find their way back to the hive.
questions.explanation: Weakened memory and lost bees are harmful effects.

distractors.why: Salutary means producing good effects, the opposite of what the research found.
Negligible means too slight to matter, but the effects were serious.
Inadvertent means unintended; the sentence needs a word about harm, not intent.

definition: to flood, or to overwhelm with a huge amount of something

examples.text: Rising seas could inundate low islands within a century.
After the announcement, volunteers inundated the recruiting offices.
The bakery was inundated with orders the week before Thanksgiving.

confused.note: Inundate means to flood or overwhelm; innovate means to introduce something new.

questions.passage: The tiny observatory had expected a few dozen visitors for the eclipse. Instead it was ______: more than four thousand people arrived, and cars lined the mountain road for six miles.
questions.explanation: Thousands arriving where dozens were expected overwhelmed the observatory.

distractors.why: Relegated means pushed to a lower position, which does not fit a crowd arriving.
Vindicated means proved right, which the passage does not describe.
Depleted means emptied or used up, the opposite of being flooded with visitors.

definition: large in amount or number

examples.text: The geologist took copious notes at every stop along the canyon.
Copious rainfall that spring produced the best harvest in a decade.
She arrived with copious snacks for the three-hour drive.

confused.note: Copious means plentiful; it has no connection to making a copy.

questions.passage: Darwin was a ______ correspondent. Over his lifetime he exchanged roughly fifteen thousand letters with gardeners, sailors, pigeon breeders, and fellow naturalists around the world.
questions.explanation: Fifteen thousand letters is a very large quantity.

distractors.why: Reticent means reluctant to communicate, the opposite of his letter writing.
Sporadic means occasional and irregular, which does not fit thousands of letters.
Cursory means hasty and shallow; the evidence given is about quantity.

definition: to publicly support or argue for something

examples.text: Suffragists advocated a constitutional amendment for decades before it passed.
Many doctors advocate regular exercise as the best defense against heart disease.
I advocated for a later start time at the student council meeting.

confused.note: Advocate means to argue for something; abdicate means to give up a throne or a duty.

questions.passage: Unlike colleagues who favor building new reservoirs, the hydrologist has long ______ a cheaper approach: repairing the leaking pipes that already waste a fifth of the city's water.
questions.explanation: She has argued publicly in favor of the cheaper approach.

distractors.why: Repudiated means rejected, but this is the approach she favors.
Lamented means mourned or regretted, which does not fit a plan she supports.
Emulated means imitated; she argues for the approach, she does not copy it.

definition: not obvious; delicate and hard to notice

examples.text: The author plants subtle clues that only make sense on a second reading.
The instrument detects subtle shifts in a star's brightness.
There was a subtle hint of cinnamon in the hot chocolate.

confused.note: Subtle (the b is silent) means delicate or not obvious; a subtitle is a secondary title or on-screen text.

questions.passage: To most listeners the two recordings sound identical. A trained musician, however, will notice ______ differences, such as a slightly slower tempo in the second movement and a softer attack on the opening chord.
questions.explanation: Differences that only a trained ear notices are slight and hard to detect.

distractors.why: Blatant means obvious, but most listeners cannot hear these differences.
Arbitrary means random or unreasoned, which does not describe small differences.
Egregious means shockingly bad, far too strong for small variations in tempo.

definition: able to express thoughts clearly in words

examples.text: The movement needed an articulate leader who could explain its goals to the press.
The narrator is an unusually articulate ten-year-old who loves long words.
Even when nervous, my lab partner stays calm and articulate during presentations.

confused.note: Articulate means clear in speech; eloquent adds beauty and the power to move listeners.

questions.passage: The witness was calm and ______. She answered each of the lawyer's questions in complete, well-organized sentences, and jurors later said they never had trouble following her account.
questions.explanation: Clear, organized answers that are easy to follow show skill in expressing thoughts.

distractors.why: Incoherent means unclear and disorganized, the opposite of her testimony.
Taciturn means saying very little, but she answered fully.
Belligerent means hostile, which contradicts "calm."

definition: so satisfied with yourself or a situation that you stop trying or stop being careful

examples.text: The complacent empire ignored reports of unrest on its borders.
Years without an outbreak made health officials complacent about vaccination.
After three easy wins, our team grew complacent and skipped practice.

confused.note: Complacent means self-satisfied; complaisant means eager to please others.

questions.passage: After a decade as the market leader, the phone maker had grown ______. Its executives dismissed a rival's touch-screen design as a fad and saw no reason to change a product that was selling so well.
questions.explanation: Dismissing a rival because sales are good shows smug self-satisfaction.

distractors.why: Vigilant means watchful, which the executives were not.
Pragmatic means practical and realistic; ignoring a real threat is neither.
Diffident means lacking confidence, but the executives were overconfident.

definition: intended for or understood by only a small group with special knowledge

examples.text: The lecture on esoteric points of string theory lost most of the audience.
The poem is packed with esoteric references to medieval alchemy.
My sister and her friends trade esoteric jokes about a video game I have never played.

confused.note: Esoteric means understood by few; exotic means strikingly foreign or unusual.

questions.passage: The journal was once criticized for publishing articles so ______ that only a few dozen specialists could follow them. Its new editor has asked every author to add a summary written for general readers.
questions.explanation: Articles that only a few specialists can follow are meant for a small expert group.

distractors.why: Lucid means clear, which would not draw this criticism.
Mundane means ordinary and dull; the criticism is about difficulty for outsiders.
Superfluous means unnecessary, which is not the criticism described.

definition: the quality of using few words or lasting a short time

examples.text: The poem's power lies in its brevity: three lines and not a wasted word.
The brevity of the Gettysburg Address surprised a crowd used to two-hour speeches.
Given the brevity of lunch period, I just grabbed a sandwich.

confused.note: Brevity means shortness; levity means lightness or humor, often at a serious time.

questions.passage: Editors at the newspaper prize ______. Reporters are told that no story should run longer than six hundred words and that any sentence that can lose a word should lose it.
questions.explanation: A word limit and trimmed sentences show that shortness is valued.

distractors.why: Verbosity means wordiness, the opposite of what the editors want.
Levity means humor or lightness; it only sounds like the right word.
Candor means honesty, which word limits do not address.

definition: changing mood or behavior suddenly and without good reason

examples.text: The capricious queen rewards a servant one day and banishes him the next.
Mountain weather is capricious, shifting from sun to hail in minutes.
Our capricious cat demands to be petted and then swats the hand that pets her.

confused.note: Capricious stresses sudden changes of mind; arbitrary stresses decisions made without reason or system.

questions.passage: Staff at the gallery never knew what to expect from its owner. She was ______, praising an exhibition lavishly on Monday and ordering it taken down on Tuesday for reasons she never explained.
questions.explanation: Reversing her opinion overnight without explanation shows sudden, unreasoned changes.

distractors.why: Steadfast means firm and unchanging, the opposite of her behavior.
Benevolent means kind; the passage is about unpredictability, not kindness.
Meticulous means careful about detail, which the passage does not address.

definition: to come together and form one group or mass

examples.text: Droplets in a cloud coalesce until they are heavy enough to fall as rain.
The scattered protest groups coalesced into a single national movement.
Our random ideas finally coalesced into a plan for the science fair.

confused.note: Coalesce means to come together into one; collapse means to fall down or fail.

questions.passage: At first the settlement was little more than a dozen farms spread across the valley. Over the next century, as roads linked them and a market opened at the crossroads, these farms gradually ______ into a town.
questions.explanation: Separate farms came together to form one town.

distractors.why: Dispersed means scattered apart, the opposite of forming a town.
Dwindled means shrank, but the farms grew into something larger.
Digressed means strayed from a topic, which does not apply to farms.

definition: unwilling to speak freely or share thoughts and feelings

examples.text: The reticent narrator tells us everything about the town and almost nothing about himself.
The general was reticent about the defeat and left it out of his memoirs.
My brother is reticent about his grades, which usually means they slipped.

confused.note: Reticent means unwilling to speak; reluctant means unwilling to do something in general.

questions.passage: In interviews the novelist will discuss her characters for hours. About her own childhood, however, she is ______, answering personal questions with a word or two before changing the subject.
questions.explanation: One-word answers and changing the subject show unwillingness to talk about herself.

distractors.why: Loquacious means very talkative, which describes her only on other subjects.
Eloquent means expressive and persuasive, but she barely answers.
Candid means open and frank, the opposite of deflecting questions.

definition: quick and cheerful readiness to do something

examples.text: The volunteers answered the call with alacrity, filling the ranks in a single day.
Offered a seat by the fire, the weary traveler accepts with alacrity.
When Dad offered to drive us to the concert, we accepted with alacrity.

confused.note: Alacrity means eager speed; clarity means clearness.

questions.passage: The interns had expected to spend the summer filing papers. So when the lead scientist invited them to join the field expedition, they responded with ______, signing up before she had finished describing it.
questions.explanation: Signing up before she finished speaking shows eager, speedy willingness.

distractors.why: Reluctance means unwillingness, the opposite of their response.
Trepidation means fear or anxiety, but the interns were eager.
Disdain means contempt, which does not describe eager acceptance.

definition: a difference between two things that should be the same

examples.text: The team traced the discrepancy between the two readings to a miscalibrated scale.
A discrepancy between the ship's log and the captain's letter raised suspicion.
There was a ten-dollar discrepancy between the receipt and what the cashier charged me.

confused.note: A discrepancy is a mismatch between things that should agree; a disparity is a large, often unfair, difference.

questions.passage: The auditor noticed a ______ between the two documents: the warehouse log listed 4,000 units shipped in March, while the sales report for the same month recorded only 3,400.
questions.explanation: Two records of the same shipments should match but differ.

distractors.why: Consensus means agreement, but the documents disagree.
A precedent is an earlier example used as a guide, which is not described.
A paradox is a seeming contradiction that may be true; this is a mismatch in records.

definition: to make something larger or stronger by adding to it

examples.text: The king augmented his army with soldiers hired from abroad.
The telescope's new mirror augments its ability to gather faint light.
She augments her allowance by walking the neighbors' dogs.

confused.note: Augment means to add to; it has no connection to an argument.

questions.passage: The library's budget could not cover every journal that researchers requested. To ______ its collection without spending more, the library joined a network that lets members borrow from one another.
questions.explanation: Joining the network adds to what the library can offer.

distractors.why: Deplete means to use up, the opposite of expanding a collection.
Scrutinize means to examine closely, which is not the goal described.
Relegate means to push to a lower position, which does not fit.

definition: decorated with a lot of complicated detail

examples.text: The palace's ornate ceilings were covered in gold leaf and painted angels.
Her ornate prose buries a simple plot under long, glittering sentences.
Grandma's ornate picture frame looks out of place on our plain white wall.

confused.note: Ornate means richly decorated; ornery means bad-tempered.

questions.passage: The designer's early furniture was ______, with carved vines curling up every chair leg and inlaid shell patterns on each drawer. Her later pieces, by contrast, have smooth surfaces and no decoration at all.
questions.explanation: Carved vines and inlaid patterns are heavy decoration.

distractors.why: Austere means severely plain, which describes her later work.
Mundane means ordinary; furniture this elaborate is not ordinary.
Fragile means easily broken; the contrast drawn is between decorated and plain.

definition: easy to shape, change, or influence

examples.text: Gold is so malleable that it can be hammered into sheets thinner than paper.
The young king proved malleable, and his advisers ruled in all but name.
Bread dough is most malleable right after it has rested.

confused.note: Malleable means easily shaped; malevolent means wishing harm.

questions.passage: Researchers once believed that the adult brain was fixed. They now know that it remains ______ throughout life: learning a new language at sixty, for example, physically strengthens connections between neurons.
questions.explanation: A brain that physically changes with learning can still be shaped.

distractors.why: Static means unchanging, which is the old belief the passage rejects.
Transient means short-lived, which is not the point about the brain.
Obsolete means outdated; that could describe the old belief, not the brain.

definition: to become less strong or severe

examples.text: The winds began to abate once the eye of the storm had passed.
Public anger did not abate until the unpopular tax was repealed.
I waited for the noise from the construction site to abate before starting my call.

confused.note: Abate means to lessen; abet means to help someone do something wrong.

questions.passage: Forecasters had predicted that the heat wave would break by Tuesday. Instead, temperatures showed no sign of ______, climbing past forty degrees for the sixth day in a row.
questions.explanation: Temperatures kept climbing, so the heat was not lessening.

distractors.why: Escalating means increasing; "no sign of escalating" would contradict six days of climbing heat.
Coalescing means merging into one, which does not apply to temperatures.
Fluctuating means rising and falling; the passage needs a word for easing, which the forecast had led people to expect.

definition: a small, subtle difference in meaning, tone, or expression

examples.text: A good translator captures every nuance of the original poem.
The textbook's short summary misses the nuances of the treaty debate.
Texting loses the nuances of tone that a phone call carries.

confused.note: A nuance is a subtle difference; a nuisance is an annoyance.

questions.passage: The film reduces the conflict to a battle between heroes and villains. The book on which it is based has far more ______, showing how each side's leaders were torn between duty and doubt.
questions.explanation: Showing leaders with mixed motives adds subtle distinctions that the film lacks.

distractors.why: Brevity means shortness, but the book offers more complexity, not fewer words.
Consensus means agreement, which does not describe a more complex portrayal.
Levity means humor or lightness, which is not what the book adds.

definition: able to recover quickly from difficulty or damage

examples.text: Coral reefs are more resilient to warming when the surrounding water is clean.
The resilient city rebuilt its harbor within two years of the earthquake.
Kids are resilient; a week after the move, my sister had three new friends.

confused.note: Resilient means able to bounce back after harm; resistant means not affected in the first place.

questions.passage: Ecologists were surprised by how ______ the forest proved to be. Only five years after the fire, saplings covered the burned slopes, and most of the bird species recorded before the blaze had returned.
questions.explanation: Quick regrowth and returning birds show the forest recovered from damage.

distractors.why: Fragile means easily damaged and slow to recover, the opposite of what happened.
Stagnant means showing no activity or growth, but the forest regrew.
Pristine means untouched, which a burned forest is not.

definition: very many; too many to count

examples.text: A drop of pond water holds myriad tiny organisms.
The empire's roads carried goods from myriad towns and villages.
There are myriad ways to cook an egg, and my dad has tried most of them.

confused.note: Myriad means a very great number; plethora means too many, an excess.

questions.passage: A modern jetliner is not the product of one factory. Its wings, engines, seats, and wiring come from ______ suppliers, with some aircraft drawing parts from more than a thousand companies in dozens of countries.
questions.explanation: More than a thousand companies is a very large number of suppliers.

distractors.why: Scant means very few, the opposite of over a thousand.
Obsolete means outdated, which is unrelated to the number of suppliers.
Clandestine means secret, which the passage does not suggest.

definition: to accept or allow behavior that is wrong

examples.text: The governor refused to condone the seizure of the farmers' land.
The narrator does not condone her brother's theft, but she understands it.
Our teacher said she could not condone cheating, even on a practice quiz.

confused.note: To condone is to let wrongdoing pass; to condemn is to declare it wrong.

questions.passage: The coach made clear that she did not ______ rough play. Any athlete who shoved an opponent, she warned, would sit out the next match regardless of the score.
questions.explanation: Punishing every shove shows she does not accept rough play.

distractors.why: Censure means to criticize severely; "did not censure" would mean she allowed it.
Emulate means to imitate, which does not fit a coach's policy on behavior.
Elicit means to draw out; the sentence is about what she will accept.

definition: to criticize someone strongly and officially

examples.text: The senate voted to censure the member who had leaked the documents.
The town's elders censure the young teacher for letting students question the founders.
The league censured the coach for arguing with the referee.

confused.note: To censure is to criticize harshly; to censor is to remove or block material.

questions.passage: The medical board did not revoke the surgeon's license. It did, however, formally ______ him, stating in a public letter that his failure to disclose the risks to patients fell below professional standards.
questions.explanation: A public letter stating he fell below standards is strong official criticism.

distractors.why: Censor means to suppress or cut material; the board criticized him, it did not delete anything.
Commend means to praise, the opposite of the board's letter.
Vindicate means to clear of blame, but the board found fault.

definition: to officially cancel a law, order, or agreement

examples.text: Parliament rescinded the tax after merchants refused to unload their ships.
The agency rescinded its approval of the drug when new side effects appeared.
The school rescinded the phone ban after parents complained.

confused.note: Rescind means to cancel officially; it is unrelated to sending something again.

questions.passage: When the university learned that the applicant had invented two of the awards on his résumé, it moved quickly to ______ its offer of admission.
questions.explanation: The university officially withdrew an offer it had made.

distractors.why: Augment means to add to; the university took the offer away.
Corroborate means to confirm with evidence, which does not fit withdrawing an offer.
Disseminate means to spread widely, which is not what happened to the offer.

definition: friendly and pleasant

examples.text: The amiable innkeeper greets every guest as if welcoming an old friend.
Despite the tense negotiations, the two envoys remained on amiable terms.
Our amiable bus driver knows every kid's name and favorite team.

confused.note: Amiable describes a friendly person; amicable describes a friendly relationship or agreement.

questions.passage: New employees are often nervous about meeting the company's founder. They soon discover that she is ______, stopping at desks to ask about weekend plans and remembering the names of everyone's pets.
questions.explanation: Chatting warmly and remembering personal details shows friendliness.

distractors.why: Aloof means distant and cool, the opposite of her manner.
Austere means stern and severe, which she is not.
Dogmatic means rigidly opinionated, which the passage does not describe.

definition: living with strict self-discipline and without ordinary comforts

examples.text: The ascetic monks ate one meal a day and slept on bare boards.
The hero returns from the mountains thin and ascetic, uninterested in his family's wealth.
During training season, the marathoner lives an ascetic life of early nights and plain food.

confused.note: Ascetic means self-denying; aesthetic means related to beauty.

questions.passage: Though the inventor earned a fortune, her habits remained ______. She lived in two small rooms above her workshop, owned a single coat, and ate the same simple supper of bread and soup every night.
questions.explanation: Two rooms, one coat, and plain suppers show a life without comforts by choice.

distractors.why: Aesthetic relates to beauty; it only looks like the right word.
Lavish means luxurious, the opposite of how she lived.
Erratic means unpredictable, but her habits never varied.

definition: showing good judgment and sense

examples.text: A judicious use of scarce supplies kept the garrison alive through the winter.
With judicious pruning, the orchard doubled its yield.
A judicious amount of hot sauce improves the soup; half the bottle ruins it.

confused.note: Judicious means wise; judicial means related to courts and judges.

questions.passage: The editor did not cut the article in half, as some had urged, nor did she leave it untouched. Her ______ trimming removed only the three paragraphs that repeated earlier points, and the piece was stronger for it.
questions.explanation: Cutting only what was repeated shows careful good judgment.

distractors.why: Indiscriminate means done without careful choice, the opposite of her selective cuts.
Reckless means careless of consequences, but the piece improved.
Cursory means hasty; she had to read closely to find the repeated paragraphs.

definition: to use up a supply of something

examples.text: Overfishing has depleted cod stocks in the North Atlantic.
The long siege depleted the city's stores of grain.
Three hours of video calls depleted my phone's battery.

confused.note: Deplete means to use up a supply; delete means to erase.

questions.passage: Farmers in the region once drew freely on the aquifer beneath their fields. Decades of heavy pumping have so ______ it that many wells now run dry by August.
questions.explanation: Wells running dry show the underground water has been used up.

distractors.why: Replenished means refilled, but the wells are dry.
Inundated means flooded, the opposite of an aquifer running out.
Augmented means increased, which contradicts the dry wells.

partsNote: from Latin plere, "to fill": to un-fill

definition: generous and forgiving, especially toward a rival or someone less powerful

examples.text: The magnanimous victor allowed the defeated soldiers to keep their horses for spring plowing.
In the final chapter the heroine is magnanimous and forgives the cousin who cheated her.
It was magnanimous of the winner to praise the runner-up in her speech.

confused.note: Magnanimous means generous in spirit; magnificent means impressively grand.

questions.passage: After a bitter campaign, many expected the new mayor to punish officials who had worked against her. She proved ______ instead, keeping several of them in their posts and publicly thanking her opponent for his years of service.
questions.explanation: Keeping rivals in office and thanking her opponent is generous and forgiving.

distractors.why: Vindictive means seeking revenge, which is what people expected, not what she did.
Complacent means smugly self-satisfied, which is not what the passage shows.
Capricious means unpredictable in mood; her generosity was deliberate.

definition: to laugh at or speak about someone or something as ridiculous

examples.text: Newspapers derided the purchase of Alaska as a waste of money.
The older boys deride the hero's dream of becoming a poet.
Fans derided the team's new mascot until it started doing backflips.

confused.note: Deride means to mock; derive means to get something from a source.

questions.passage: When the Wright brothers announced that they had flown, several newspapers ______ the claim, with one editor joking that the brothers were better at lying than at flying.
questions.explanation: An editor's mocking joke shows the claim was ridiculed.

distractors.why: Corroborated means confirmed, but the papers made fun of the claim.
Lauded means praised, the opposite of joking that the brothers were liars.
Rescinded means officially cancelled, which newspapers cannot do to a claim.

definition: skillful and quick in using the hands or the mind

examples.text: An adroit negotiator, she won concessions from both sides without angering either.
With one adroit flick of the wrist, the thief empties the merchant's purse.
The goalie made an adroit save, tipping the ball over the bar with one hand.

confused.note: Both mean skilled; adroit adds quickness and cleverness in handling a tricky situation.

questions.passage: Reporters tried repeatedly to trap the minister into criticizing her own party. She was too ______ for them, answering each question with a joke or a compliment that revealed nothing.
questions.explanation: Slipping out of every trap shows quick, clever skill.

distractors.why: Inept means clumsy and unskilled, but she handled the reporters well.
Candid means frank and open, yet her answers revealed nothing.
Belligerent means hostile; she deflected with humor and charm.

partsNote: from French "à droit," according to right

definition: difficult to understand

examples.text: The paper's abstruse mathematics defeated all but a few readers.
Critics complained that the poet's later work had grown abstruse and cold.
The tax form's abstruse instructions sent me straight to the help line.

confused.note: Abstruse describes ideas that are hard to understand; obtuse describes a person who is slow to understand.

questions.passage: The philosopher's first book was widely praised for its clarity and plain style. Her second, filled with invented terms and page-long sentences, struck most reviewers as needlessly ______.
questions.explanation: Invented terms and very long sentences make a book hard to understand.

distractors.why: Lucid means clear, which described her first book.
Obtuse describes a person who is slow to understand, not writing that is hard to follow.
Terse means brief and clipped, but the sentences ran a page long.

definition: working hard and carefully over time

examples.text: Diligent record keeping allowed the team to spot a trend across twenty years.
The diligent clerk copied every charter in the archive by hand.
She was diligent about practicing scales, and it showed at the recital.

confused.note: Diligent means steadily hardworking; dilatory means slow and tending to delay.

questions.passage: Talent alone did not explain the young cellist's rise. Her teachers pointed instead to how ______ she was: she practiced four hours a day, kept a notebook of every correction, and never arrived at a lesson unprepared.
questions.explanation: Daily practice, careful notes, and constant preparation show steady hard work.

distractors.why: Complacent means self-satisfied and no longer trying, the opposite of her habits.
Capricious means changeable and unpredictable, but her effort was constant.
Gregarious means sociable, which the passage does not discuss.

definition: polite respect that leads you to accept another person's wishes or opinion

examples.text: Out of deference to the elderly emperor, the generals delayed their plan.
The young clerk treats his employer with a deference that borders on fear.
In deference to my grandmother, we turned off our phones at dinner.

confused.note: Deference is respectful yielding; difference is the way things are unlike.

questions.passage: The committee's younger members had doubts about the plan. Out of ______ to its author, a scientist with fifty years of experience, they kept those doubts to themselves and voted to approve it.
questions.explanation: Staying silent out of respect for a senior scientist is respectful yielding.

distractors.why: Defiance means open resistance, but they kept quiet and approved the plan.
Antipathy means strong dislike, which would not make them hold back criticism.
Alacrity means cheerful eagerness, which does not fit members who had doubts.

partsNote: to carry oneself down, to yield
